ADS-C in the OPDI trajectory

Version 1 — what a satellite cruise feed adds to flight-event extraction

Author

EUROCONTROL Performance Review Unit — Open Performance Data Initiative

Published

October 20, 2026

Abstract

OPDI builds every track from ADS-B state vectors. OpenSky also publishes an ADS-C feed, and the obvious hypothesis is that merging the two improves coverage and therefore milestone extraction. This paper tests it. ADS-C is merged into the state-vector frame before segmentation, so track_id sees both sources; the trajectory cleaner is made source-aware, because its twenty-second isolated-point rule would otherwise delete a feed whose median cadence is ten minutes. Both arms — ADS-B only, and ADS-B plus ADS-C — are rebuilt from the same state vectors with the same segmentation and the same detectors, and scored against EUROCONTROL APDF over the twenty aerodromes and three days of flight events version 4.

The feed is narrow and the result is correspondingly narrow. Measured over eleven days spanning 2023-09 to 2026-10, ADS-C delivers a few thousand rows a day inside OPDI’s European box at a median of several hundred seconds between reports; almost all of those rows are above FL300 and most sit west of 10°W. It carries no on_ground flag and almost nothing below ten thousand feet. The A-CDM runway family therefore cannot move, and this paper reports that as a measured null rather than omitting it.

The two feeds also do not share a clock, and neither states a position age that can be used. Comparing ADS-C reports against ADS-B interpolated to the same instant separates the two candidate explanations: the feeds agree about where the track is to within a few metres across track while disagreeing by hundreds of metres along it, which is a timing offset and not a position error. That offset is a property of the individual airframe rather than of the feed, so no global correction is applied and the paper says why.

Every figure is produced by benchmarks/regenerate_adsc_v1.py. Where an output is not staged the table says so in place rather than being omitted.

1 What the feed is

OpenSky publishes an ADS-C topic beside the ADS-B archive: s3a://readsb-aircraft-states/topics/readsb.aircraft.adsc.avro, hourly partitions named hour=<unix seconds>, holding snappy parquet despite the .avro in the topic name — the files carry the Avro schema org.opensky.avro.readsb.Aircraft in their footer. Partitions run from 2023-07-07 to the current hour, 982 days with 24 gaps longer than a day, and in 2026 the feed averages 22.3 of 24 hourly partitions per day. A missing hour is routine, and the ingest tolerates it by listing before reading rather than letting spark.read.parquet raise PATH_NOT_FOUND on the first absent one.

The raw ADS-C topic, by sampled day. Every band after In box is counted inside OPDI’s published European coverage box – that is the population the pipeline would ingest. Hours read matters: a day with 6 of 24 partitions present has a cadence that reflects the gap, not the feed.

Reading that table across the archive: the feed delivers 409-32206 rows a day worldwide and 140-5420 inside the coverage box, from 74-994 in-box airframes. On the three study days it is 4725-5420 in-box rows from 953-994 airframes, at a median of 543-568 seconds between reports from one aircraft. Against the 5 s resolution OPDI ingests ADS-B at, that is a feed roughly two orders of magnitude sparser.

It is also a cruise feed, and that is what bounds what it can contribute. Of the in-box rows, 94.4-98.6% are above FL300 and 65.8-83.8% sit west of 10°W — the North Atlantic corner of the box. The whole box sees 1-67 rows a day below ten thousand feet, and on_ground is true for 0 rows across every day sampled. There is also no redelivery to clean up: 0 exact duplicates in total, so the ingest’s deduplication has never had anything to remove.

That table is the reason this study carries five fields and not twenty-five. A reader would reasonably expect an ADS-C report to bring indicated airspeed, Mach, outside air temperature, wind, the selected altitude from the FMS, and the aircraft’s registration and type. The readsb record has a column for each of them, and every one measured 0.0% on all eleven days. They are not discarded by OPDI; they are not there. The same is true of alt_geom, so an ADS-C sample contributes barometric altitude and no geometric altitude at all. nic, rc, seen, seen_pos and rssi are present but constant — zero, zero, zero, zero and −49.5 — which makes them defaults rather than measurements, and they are not carried as if they were.

Two step changes are visible there, and neither is documented upstream. track, gs and baro_rate are empty until somewhere between 2025-03 and 2025-09; flight, squawk and on_ground until between 2026-03 and 2026-06. Before roughly 2025-09 the feed is position and barometric altitude and nothing else. For this study that is harmless — the three study days are fully populated, and the callsign is deliberately dropped in any case — but a merged arm over 2023 or 2024 would write ADS-C rows with NULL velocity and NULL vert_rate, and any speed-based detector would see NULL rather than a value on those rows. If the study period ever moves back, that moves with it.

2 How it is merged

Decision Value Where
Merge point Before segmentation TrackProcessor._merge_adsc
Default Off (adsc.enabled = False) AdscConfig
ADS-C callsign NULL osn_adsc.to_opdi_schema
Shadow window −60 s … +60 s AdscConfig.shadow_{before,after}_seconds
Global time correction 0 s (off) AdscConfig.time_offset_seconds
Thinning applied to ADS-C None AdscIngestion.ingest_from_s3
Isolated-point rule Exempt for ADS-C CleaningConfig.sparse_sources
Stale-broadcast rule Exempt for ADS-C CleaningConfig.sparse_sources
Dedup tie-break ADS-B wins drop_duplicate_statevectors
Derivative-spike filter Unchanged mask_derivative_spikes
Segment split Unchanged, 300 s CleaningConfig.segment_gap_seconds

Four of those need an argument rather than an assertion.

Why before segmentation. The hypothesis is about coverage and track continuity, and both are properties of track_id — which _add_track_id assigns from the frame it is handed. Merging afterwards could only attach ADS-C to tracks ADS-B had already drawn, which answers a different question: which ADS-B tracks can ADS-C be attached to, rather than what tracks do the two feeds make together. A test reads that ordering off the source of process_month so it cannot drift.

Why the callsign is dropped. The feed’s flight field carries the IATA commercial number — LH133, AF805, AY68 — and ADS-B broadcasts the ICAO callsign, DLH133. The production segmentation arm (A9, debounced) breaks a track when the last non-blank callsign changes, so carrying flight through would trip that break at every ADS-C sample and split precisely the tracks the merge exists to join. A9 bridges NULLs by design, with F.last(..., ignorenulls=True), so NULL removes a false signal rather than losing a true one. An IATA-to-ICAO mapping would recover the field; it was not attempted here.

Why the cleaner had to change. CleaningConfig.isolated_max_gap_seconds is 20 s, and mask_isolated_points NULLs any value whose nearest same-column neighbour is further away than that on both sides. At a cadence of several hundred seconds that is every ADS-C sample, in every column it touches. Left unexempted, step 02a would delete the position, altitude and speed of the entire feed it had just been handed — and the merged arm would then score identically to the baseline for a reason having nothing to do with the hypothesis. A test asserts exactly that failure with the exemption switched off, so the result cannot be quietly reintroduced.

Why track_id changes, and what that costs. Enabling the merge is a fourth track_id boundary after legacy → A8 → A9. Like those it is silent to a joiner — an empty join, not an error — and that is why both arms of this study live under s3a://eurocontrol/opdi/research/adsc/ and the flag ships off. No published table moves.

3 Whether the two clocks agree

ADS-B and ADS-C arrive over different links and neither states a position age that can be used. ADS-B’s last_pos_update is real but small. ADS-C’s seen and seen_pos are constant zero — the feed asserts that every report is current — and the readsb record does not expose the ADS-C report’s own time-of-position, so there is nothing in band to correct from. The skew was therefore measured.

For each ADS-C report with an ADS-B sample of the same airframe within 60 s on both sides, the ADS-B position is interpolated to the ADS-C timestamp and the offset decomposed against the direction the ADS-B pair actually moved — not against the broadcast heading, which in wind is not where the aircraft is going. Cross-track is what the two feeds disagree about that no timing explanation can absorb; along-track divided by ground speed is the implied time offset. A position error is isotropic and lands in both; a timing error lands only along track.

Four things follow, in order.

It is timing, not position. The along-track disagreement is 415.4 m against 8.7 m across track, a ratio of 47.6. A position error is isotropic and would land equally in both, so a ratio of that size cannot be one. The two feeds agree about where the track is to within a few metres.

ADS-B carry-forward explains the tail, not the centre. The OSN archive carries positions forward, which biases this measurement in exactly the direction observed, so the alternative has to be settled from the data rather than argued away. ADS-B’s own position age is 0.34 s at the median – about 82.3 m at cruise, far too little to account for a 415.4 m along-track displacement – and it correlates with the implied offset at only 0.21, so it is not driving the central tendency. But it reaches 152.3 s at the extreme, which is 36.6 km at cruise, and that is more than enough to produce the largest offsets in the per-airframe table below. The honest division: the median is ADS-C skew, and the tail is at least partly a stale reference. The prototype behind this study saw a maximum age of 0.92 s and concluded carry-forward was excluded outright; at 17x more pairs that conclusion does not survive and is narrowed here.

It is one number per aircraft, not one number – and a noisy one. Within-airframe standard deviations span 0.00-44.76 s, so some airframes are stable and others are not; between airframes the median offset runs from -184.60 s to +58.69 s. The spread between aircraft dwarfs anything a single value could track, which is why AdscConfig.time_offset_seconds ships at zero: a single constant would be wrong for nearly every aircraft and would actively damage the ones that are already synchronised. A per-airframe offset, estimated on coverage-overlap data and applied where ADS-B is absent, is the real fix; it needs a stability study across weeks before it could be believed, and 293 airframes over three days cannot support one. It is not attempted here.

It matters less than the alternative. At a cruise speed of about 240 m/s the median offset is roughly 338.7 m. The alternative to having an ADS-C sample at all is a straight line interpolated across a reception hole of several hundred seconds, whose own error is tens of kilometres. The skew is therefore a correction worth reporting and not a reason to withhold the merge.

One thing the skew does not reach: the derivative-spike filter. CleaningConfig.latlon_d1_max_deg_s is 0.01 deg/s, about 1,100 m/s of apparent ground speed, and a few hundred metres of displacement across a several-hundred -second gap adds of the order of 0.001 deg/s. The filter is three orders of magnitude away from seeing this error, so it neither corrects it nor is damaged by it — which is also why no source guard was added there. Adding one would have been machinery for a risk that is not present.

Reading those tables in order. Something arrived: 12,941 ADS-C rows survived cleaning – 0.0085% of all rows in the merged arm, about one in twelve thousand – reaching 3,832 of 141,232 tracks (2.7%). The track count moved up 795 – 141,232 against 140,437 – and decomposes into 905 new tracks for airframes ADS-B never heard in the window – trajectories that had no baseline counterpart at all – against a net -110 among the tracks both arms share. The population they have in common got smaller, which is what bridging does; the headline rise is new coverage, not fragmentation. 12,498 ADS-C samples closed a reception hole, counted strictly: more than 300 s from an ADS-B sample on both sides, so a sample sitting inside a dense stretch and seen as isolated from one direction does not qualify. The merge-neutrality guard reads 9,244 two-callsign tracks in the merged arm against 9,244 in the baseline – a track holding two distinct real callsigns is two flights fused into one, the way this change could do real harm.

One limit on that last pair of numbers, and on the net figure above: both are aggregates. A net change of zero among shared tracks is consistent with no change at all and equally with equal numbers of joins and splits, so these rule out a dominant effect rather than an absent one.

Read what this table scores before reading what it says. APDF can score 4 milestones – AIBT, ALDT, AOBT, ATOT – and every one of them belongs to the A-CDM and runway family. The families where ADS-C could physically contribute (first_seen, last_seen, the flight-level crossings, and ADEP/ADES through the flight list) are not in the reference’s vocabulary at all: APDF records aerodrome movements, not the moment an oceanic track begins.

So this chapter can confirm the predicted null and it cannot detect the gain. That is a property of the reference, not a result. The coverage ADS-C adds is measured in the previous chapter – new tracks, closed holes, track-hours – and nothing APDF holds can corroborate or contradict it. A reader who takes a flat table here as ‘ADS-C adds nothing’ has drawn a conclusion the instrument cannot support.

Whatever those tables show, one thing cannot be read out of them, and it is worth stating before they are read at all: the A-CDM and runway families could not have moved. ADS-C has no on_ground flag that is ever true, the whole coverage box sees 1-67 of its rows a day below ten thousand feet, and its cadence is several hundred seconds against detectors that interpolate a runway-threshold crossing between adjacent samples. A flat row for ATOT, ALDT, AOBT or AIBT is the expected outcome of adding this feed, not a failure of the detector or of the measurement. The families where a change is physically possible are the ones anchored at the edges of coverage — first_seen, last_seen, the flight-level crossings, and ADEP/ADES through the flight list for North Atlantic arrivals.

And for any event that did move, the move is not automatically an improvement. Nothing in the pipeline prevents an event being interpolated between an ADS-B and an ADS-C sample, so an event derived across that boundary inherits the along-track displacement measured in the previous chapter. See the limitations below.

6 What this does not measure

Each of these is a measurement that was not made, not a result:

  • The reference cannot score the families ADS-C can reach. APDF holds aerodrome movements: ATOT, AOBT, AIBT, ALDT. first_seen, last_seen, the flight-level crossings and ADEP/ADES are outside its vocabulary, so the milestone chapter confirms the predicted null on the A-CDM family and is structurally incapable of detecting a gain at the coverage edge. The trajectory chapter is the only evidence for that gain, and it has no independent reference to be checked against. Closing this would need a different reference – Network Manager flight plans for the oceanic entry fixes, say – not more days of APDF.
  • Only Europe. Scoring is inside EUROPE_BBOX, and most of the in-box ADS-C rows sit in its Atlantic corner. The feed is global; a worldwide arm would see far more of it, and APDF could not score it.
  • Only June 2026, three days. The flight-events-v4 period, chosen for comparability. ADS-C volumes in 2023–2024 are not scored, and the feed carried fewer columns then.
  • No shadow-window sweep. −60/+60 s is a reasoned default, not a tuned one. A wider window drops more ADS-C; a narrower one admits near-duplicate positions. At the measured skew a symmetric window already catches every duplicate pair, so the asymmetry is what makes the time base explicit rather than a fix for a present failure.
  • No per-airframe time correction, and no stability study of the skew. The time-synchronisation chapter measures the offset on three days and a few tens of airframes. Whether an airframe’s offset is stable across weeks — the precondition for correcting it — is not measured here.
  • No IATA-to-ICAO callsign recovery. The feed’s flight field is discarded rather than mapped, so ADS-C contributes no callsign evidence to segmentation or to the flight list.
  • Nothing stops an event being interpolated across a source boundary. segment_id splits at 300 s coverage holes and is read by no detector — grep -rn segment_id src/opdi/pipeline/ finds it in two comments. An event derived between an ADS-B and an ADS-C sample therefore inherits the along-track displacement. This is pre-existing: the same detectors already interpolate across thirty-minute ADS-B holes. Making segment_id load-bearing would change published detector behaviour, so it is named here as a follow-up rather than changed on this branch.
  • The MLAT topic is untouched. readsb.aircraft.mlat.avro is a second unused OpenSky source, denser than ADS-C — of the order of 374 objects a day — but starting only at 2026-05-18. It is multilateration, not ADS-C, and is out of scope.
  • No measurement of ADS-C positional accuracy. nic and rc are constant zero in the feed, so the usual integrity containment bounds are unavailable. Nothing here establishes how accurate an ADS-C position is, only what including it changes — and the cross-track figure bounds the disagreement, which is not the same thing as an error.

7 Reproducing this

# 1. The two arms. ~6 cluster-hours. Not regenerated by the entrypoint.
#    Day-major, not step-major: step 01 keeps a three-day sliding window and
#    drops what the window has passed, so ingesting every day before
#    segmenting any of them would hand day 05 a window two-thirds absent.
export PYSPARK_DRIVER_PYTHON=$PWD/.venv310/bin/python
unset PYSPARK_PYTHON OPDI_WAREHOUSE
for d in 2026-06-05 2026-06-06 2026-06-07; do
  .venv310/bin/python -u benchmarks/run_adsc_day.py --day $d --arm both
done

# 2. Every figure on this page.
.venv310/bin/python -u benchmarks/regenerate_adsc_v1.py

# 3. This page.
cd ../opdi-portal/papers && quarto render adsc-fusion-v1/index.qmd
